newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan youth murder exposes education problems.
newsitem.headline: Japan youth murder exposes education problems.

text.p: Japan's draconian education system has come under a harsh spotlight once again after the arrest of a 14-year-old boy suspected in the brutal murder of a schoolchild.

While police were investigating the motive for the decapitation murder that shocked the nation, experts put at least part of the blame on strict discipline at school and called for an overhaul of the education system.
"I believe that Japan's education system is in large part behind this brutal crime," said Masao Omura, honorary professor of psychology at Nihon University.
"Japan must overhaul the education system as soon as possible. If not, there could be a repetition of this vicious incident," he told Reuters.
In a letter to a local newspaper a week after the body was found last month, the killer said that he would "take revenge on the compulsory education system".

"I am not forgetting revenge for the compulsory education that has produced me as an invisible existence and on the society that has produced this compulsory education," the rambling note read in part.
Academic standards in Japanese schools have long been the envy of education leaders abroad, but some critics argue that the strict discipline often does more harm than good.

University entrance exams are an obsession in Japan, the climax of up to 15 years of high-pressure education which for some tots begins with cram schools to secure a place at a top-notch kindergarten.

The practice in large companies and the central bureaucracy of recruiting only from elite universities, coupled with Japan's "job-for-life" employment system, means that a person's career path can be largely determined at 18 by success or failure in one exam.
"Under the compulsory education system, those who are not treated well in school could become crooked," said Hiroaki Iwai, criminal psychologist at Tokyo University.
"I am sure that there are many children who are introverted and emotionally unstable. When they come under excessive pressure, they could commit such a brutal crime," he added.
Some experts also believe that far-reaching and strict rules at schools could do nothing but corner children into committing crimes.
"Schools, which suppress children with rules, serve as main sources of stress for these children," said Masashi Miyadai, professor of Sociology at Tokyo Metropolitan University.
"There is no doubt that the school system played a role in triggering the boy to commit the crime," he said.
Pupils at most public and private Japanese middle and high schools must carry school rule books which regulate their lives down to the smallest detail, including length of skirts.
Many schools try to regulate after-school life by prohibiting students from going to fast food restaurants alone or seeing students of the opposite sex.
"Teachers must be aware that there is a strong hostility among students aimed at schools," Miyadai said.
Experts warn that Japan, priding itself on being a safe society, could see more such brutal crimes committed by teenagers.
"Up until today, cases like this extremely sadistic crime among teenagers have been rare in Japan," Nihon University's Omura said.
"The case gave us a warning that this is just the beginning," he added.
